judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 420, which makes school districts report on force used by their own police. A district that employs school police, and a charter school that contracts for them, must publish a report each school year. The report covers incidents involving a baton, a chemical agent such as pepper spray, or a stun device. For each one it must say where it happened and whether it was during the school day or at a school event. It must also give the age, race, gender and ethnicity of the people force was used on, with no names. The report goes on the district's own website. The bill only requires the numbers to be published. It does not limit when force may be used, and it sets no penalty for failing to publish. The Nevada Senate passed it 15-6. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 460, which gives parents a form for naming who should raise their child if they cannot. A parent signs the form in front of two adult witnesses who have no stake in the family's money, and has it notarized. The parent can name a first choice and a backup, and can say they do not want a for-profit guardian appointed. A court has to take the form into account when it picks a guardian. The form does not hand anyone custody. The person named still has to ask a court to appoint them. The bill also lets a court treat temporary guardianship as best for a child when a parent is separated from that child by a federal immigration order. Registering the form with the Secretary of State becomes free. The Nevada Senate passed it 16-4. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Assembly Bill 540, which puts $133 million of state money into a new housing fund. The Nevada Attainable Housing Account is run by the state Housing Division. The plan set out in the bill is $83 million for building housing and buying land, $25 million to help essential workers buy a home, and $25 million to reward local governments that waive fees. Every dollar has to be matched by private, local or federal money. The bill also orders up to $50 million in state bonds for roads and pipes serving these projects. Counties and cities must set up a faster approval track for them. The bill widens who counts as needing help, reaching households earning up to 150 percent of the local median income. It also drops a rule that had aimed local fee relief at lower-income projects. The Nevada Senate passed it 15-6. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 157, which makes testing of cannabis a requirement rather than a choice. The Cannabis Compliance Board could already write testing rules if it wanted to. The bill says it must. The rules have to send samples from each lot to an independent laboratory. They have to follow a national sampling standard and take set minimum sample weights, starting at 10 grams for a lot under 5 pounds. The bill does not say what the labs must test for, and sets no pass or fail limits. It leaves those to the Board. The Nevada Assembly passed it 31-11. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 370, which puts a deadline on replacing the ownership papers for a manufactured home. A certificate of title is the document that proves who owns a manufactured or mobile home. When the old one is lost or withheld, the owner asks the state Housing Division for a new one. Before this bill the Division could take as long as it liked and did not have to explain a refusal. The bill gives it 45 days to issue the title or turn the request down. A refusal has to come with written reasons within 10 days. The Division must also set up a faster track for people who pay for it. The bond and inspection an owner needs for the backup route do not change. The Nevada Senate passed it 16-5. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 39, which sets up a state loan fund for work that reduces damage from disasters. The Nevada Hazard Mitigation Revolving Loan Account is run by the Division of Emergency Management. Nevada needs a fund like this before the federal government will give it disaster money under the STORM Act. Only local and tribal governments may borrow from it, not homeowners or businesses. Projects paid for by these loans must use prevailing wages and competitive bidding. The bill puts no money in the account. It fills only if federal grants arrive and a later legislature adds a state match. The Nevada Senate passed it 13-8. and the bill was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 424, which charges private ambulance companies a fee and sends the money back as higher Medicaid rates. The fee is a share of what a company collects for emergency trips in Nevada, capped at 5.5 percent unless a higher rate is needed to draw the federal match. Ambulance services run by a government or a tribe do not pay it. At least 90 percent of the money has to go to better Medicaid pay for private ambulance companies. The point is to draw federal matching money the state could not otherwise claim. The fee stops if the federal money does not come, or if the state cuts its own ambulance funding, and companies get refunds. A company with few Medicaid patients can still pay more than it gets back. The Nevada Senate passed it 16-4. and the bill was signed into law.
